Andromache. The wife of Hector and mother of their infant son Astyanax, she stands as the tragic image of the devoted woman watching helplessly as her family and city are destroyed by war. Deeply in love with her husband, Andromache was also terrified for their son, knowing that his fate was bound to Troy's own destruction. In one of literature's most poignant scenes, she watched Hector depart for battle in the Iliad, fully aware that his doom was written in fate itself. When she learned of his death at Achilles' hands, she witnessed it from Troy's walls, experiencing the moment that shattered her world. After Troy's fall, Andromache was enslaved to Neoptolemus, Achilles' son, and forced to bear his children, transforming her from a princess into a captive concubine. Her final role exemplified the fate of all Trojan women after the city's destruction. Despite the horrors inflicted upon her, Andromache came to symbolize feminine resilience and the depths of maternal devotion, standing as a testament to human dignity even amid the devastation of war.
